overview: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) in Databricks is implemented through Unity Catalog, the centralized governance layer that controls who can access which data objects (catalogs, schemas, tables, views, functions, volumes) and what they can do with them.

Access is expressed as GRANT/REVOKE of privileges (such as SELECT, MODIFY, USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA) to principals (users, groups, service principals) on securable objects arranged in a three-level namespace: catalog.schema.object.

Unity Catalog enforces a privilege hierarchy with inheritance and object ownership, and the strong best practice is to grant privileges to groups rather than individual users to keep access manageable, auditable, and aligned with least privilege.
learningObjectives: Understand Unity Catalog principals, securable objects, privileges, and the three-level namespace.
Master GRANT/REVOKE syntax, the privilege hierarchy and inheritance, and the role of object ownership.
Apply group-based RBAC and least-privilege best practices to design maintainable, auditable access control.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: RBAC in Databricks Unity Catalog is an access-control model in which privileges on securable objects are granted to principals (users, groups, service principals), where privileges inherit down a hierarchy (metastore -> catalog -> schema -> object) and a principal can perform an action on an object only if it holds the required privilege plus the traversal privileges (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA) on all ancestors, subject to object ownership which confers full control.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of Unity Catalog as a building with floors (catalogs), rooms (schemas), and filing cabinets (tables). RBAC is the keycard system: instead of cutting a key for every person, you create groups like 'Analysts' and give the group keycards that open the right floors, rooms, and cabinets. People inherit access by being in the group, and you must hold a keycard for the floor and room (USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA) before you can even reach a cabinet inside.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Early Databricks used workspace-scoped table access control lists tied to individual clusters, which were inconsistent across workspaces. Unity Catalog, launched in 2022, introduced account-level, centralized RBAC with a metastore shared across workspaces, identity federation from the account, and ANSI-SQL GRANT/REVOKE, bringing Databricks governance in line with mature data-warehouse RBAC models like Snowflake and traditional RDBMS.

whyItMatters.business: Centralized RBAC enforces compliance (GDPR, HIPAA, SOX), proves who can access sensitive data during audits, and reduces the risk and cost of data breaches and regulatory fines.
whyItMatters.engineering: A single, consistent access model across all workspaces removes per-cluster, per-workspace ACL drift, making access reproducible and easy to reason about and automate.
whyItMatters.scalability: Group-based grants and hierarchical inheritance let one grant cover thousands of users and many objects, so access management scales with the organization instead of exploding into per-user, per-table entries.
whyItMatters.cost: Reducing manual, error-prone access administration and avoiding over-provisioned access lowers operational overhead and limits the blast radius (and cost) of accidental or malicious data exposure.
whyItMatters.reliability: Deterministic, inheritance-based permissions reduce 'works for me but not for them' access bugs and make pipelines and dashboards behave consistently for all members of a role.

coreComponents.name: Principals (Users, Groups, Service Principals)
coreComponents.definition: The identities to which privileges are granted: individual users, groups of identities, and service principals used by automated jobs and applications.
coreComponents.purpose: To represent the 'who' in an access grant so privileges can be assigned at the right granularity.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Account-level identities are federated to workspaces; groups aggregate users/service principals; service principals carry permissions for non-interactive workloads.

coreComponents.name: Securable Objects and the Three-Level Namespace
coreComponents.definition: The 'what' that privileges apply to, organized as metastore -> catalog -> schema -> {table, view, function, volume, external location, storage credential, model}.
coreComponents.purpose: To define the scope of a grant, from an entire catalog down to a single table or function.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Objects are referenced as catalog.schema.object; higher-level objects act as containers whose privileges can be inherited by children.

coreComponents.name: Privileges and Ownership
coreComponents.definition: The 'what action' component: privileges like SELECT, MODIFY, USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, CREATE TABLE, EXECUTE, plus object ownership which grants full control over an object and its children.
coreComponents.purpose: To express least-privilege access and to designate who can manage and re-grant an object.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Privileges are granted/revoked via GRANT/REVOKE; the owner can ALTER, DROP, and GRANT on the object; ownership should typically be a group, not an individual.
coreComponents.examples: GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders TO `data-analysts`; ALTER TABLE ... OWNER TO `sales-admins`.

internalWorking: When a principal issues a query, Unity Catalog resolves the fully qualified object name and checks the principal's effective privileges, which are the union of grants made directly to the principal and to every group it belongs to (recursively).

Access requires the action privilege on the target object AND the traversal privileges on all ancestors: USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the schema; without these the object is not even visible, so SELECT alone is insufficient.

Privileges inherit downward: a grant on a catalog or schema applies to current and future child objects, while the object owner implicitly has full control and is the only one (besides metastore admins and those with MANAGE) who can grant privileges or transfer ownership; REVOKE removes a specific grant but does not override inheritance from a higher level.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Account Identities (users/groups/service principals) -> Unity Catalog Metastore -> Catalog (USE CATALOG) -> Schema (USE SCHEMA) -> Object (SELECT/MODIFY/EXECUTE) with Ownership conferring full control and inheritance flowing top-down
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. The 'data-analysts' group is granted USE CATALOG on 'prod', USE SCHEMA on 'prod.sales', and SELECT on 'prod.sales.orders'.
2. Alice, a member of 'data-analysts', runs SELECT * FROM prod.sales.orders.
3. Unity Catalog computes Alice's effective privileges as the union of her group memberships and finds USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, and SELECT all present.
4. The query is authorized; if any traversal privilege were missing, the object would be invisible and the query would fail with a permission error even though SELECT was granted.

keyTerminology.meaning: Privileges granted on a higher-level securable (catalog or schema) automatically apply to its current and future child objects.
keyTerminology.importance: It lets you grant access to whole catalogs/schemas in one statement rather than enumerating every table, simplifying management.

keyTerminology.meaning: Privileges that allow a principal to reference and traverse into a catalog or schema; they do not by themselves grant data access.
keyTerminology.importance: Required ancestors-must-be-traversable rule: without USE on the parents, SELECT on the table is useless.

keyTerminology.meaning: The principal designated as owner of a securable; the owner has full control (ALTER, DROP, GRANT) over that object and its children.
keyTerminology.importance: Owners can re-grant access, so ownership should be assigned to admin groups, not individuals, to avoid orphaned or over-powered access.

importantConcepts.explanation: Grant principals only the minimum privileges needed for their role and nothing more. In Unity Catalog this means default-deny, granting USE + SELECT to read-only analysts, USE + MODIFY/CREATE only to engineers who write, and reserving ownership/MANAGE for small admin groups.

Map organizational roles to Unity Catalog groups (synced from your identity provider), grant privileges to groups rather than users, and manage individual access purely by group membership. This keeps grants stable as people join and leave, makes audits simple, and prevents the explosion of per-user grants.

variationsAndTypes: **Read-only role:** USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT (typical analyst).
**Read-write role:** adds MODIFY and CREATE TABLE/CREATE SCHEMA (typical engineer).
**Admin/owner role:** object ownership or MANAGE plus catalog-level grants (typical data platform team).
**Service principal role:** scoped privileges for automated jobs (e.g., SELECT on source, MODIFY on target) with no interactive login.
advantages: **Centralized and consistent:** One metastore enforces the same access model across all workspaces.
**Scales via inheritance and groups:** A single grant can cover many objects and many users.
**Auditable:** Grants and access are logged centrally for compliance and security review.
**Standard SQL interface:** ANSI GRANT/REVOKE is familiar and automatable via Terraform/SQL.
disadvantages: **Role explosion risk:** Poorly designed roles can proliferate into many overlapping groups.
**Coarser than ABAC:** Pure RBAC cannot easily express context-dependent rules (time, location, attributes) without combining with row/column policies.
**Traversal gotcha:** Forgetting USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA causes confusing 'no access' errors despite SELECT grants.
**Ownership pitfalls:** Individual ownership creates single points of failure when people leave.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use group-based RBAC for virtually all data governance in Unity Catalog: stable organizational roles, multi-team workspaces, compliance requirements, and any environment where access must be auditable and scale with headcount.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: RBAC alone is insufficient when access must depend on data attributes or request context (e.g., row-level filters per region, dynamic PII masking); there you combine RBAC with row filters, column masks, and is_account_group_member-based policies.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: RBAC is like a corporate building with keycards. You don't cut a unique key for every employee; you create access groups (Finance, Engineering, Visitors) and program keycards so each group opens only the floors and rooms it needs. New hires simply join a group and inherit its access; leavers are removed from the group and instantly lose it. A facilities manager (owner) controls who gets which keycard.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Granting SELECT on a table is enough for a user to query it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The principal also needs USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the schema. Privileges on parents must be present to traverse to the object; without them the table is invisible despite the SELECT grant.

commonMisconceptions.myth: It's fine to grant privileges directly to individual users for convenience.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Per-user grants become unmanageable and inconsistent at scale and complicate audits and offboarding. The best practice is to grant to groups and control access solely through group membership synced from the identity provider.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Sync groups from your IdP (SCIM) and grant to groups; use catalog/schema-level grants with inheritance so adding tables or users does not require new grants.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Assign ownership to admin groups (never individuals) so access management survives personnel changes; codify grants in Terraform/SQL for reproducibility.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because Unity Catalog is account-level, access definitions persist independent of any single workspace; recreate workspaces without losing the governance model.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Audit grants via INFORMATION_SCHEMA and SHOW GRANTS, and use Unity Catalog audit logs / system tables to track access and privilege changes.
productionConsiderations.security: Apply least privilege and default-deny; reserve MANAGE/ownership for small admin groups; combine RBAC with row filters and column masks for fine-grained protection.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Group-based inheritance minimizes administrative effort and the number of grant objects, reducing operational toil and the cost of audits.
productionConsiderations.performance: Authorization checks are metadata operations with negligible query overhead; well-structured groups keep effective-privilege computation simple.

codeExamples.title: Group-based least-privilege grants across the hierarchy
codeExamples.overview: Grant a read-only analyst group and a read-write engineering group the correct combination of traversal and action privileges in Unity Catalog.
codeExamples.breakdown: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA let principals traverse into the namespace. Granting SELECT/MODIFY on the SCHEMA uses inheritance so every current and future table is covered without per-table grants. SHOW GRANTS audits effective permissions; REVOKE removes a specific grant.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: data-analysts can read prod.sales.orders (until revoked); data-engineers can read, write, and create tables across prod.sales. SHOW GRANTS lists the grants on the schema.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Granting SELECT without USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA results in 'object not found / permission denied'; granting to individual users instead of groups; revoking a table grant while a broader schema grant still confers access via inheritance.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Grant at the schema level with inheritance for whole-schema roles; grant at the table level only for exceptions. Manage membership in the IdP, not via per-user grants.

codeExamples.title: Ownership, MANAGE, and auditing effective access
codeExamples.overview: Transfer ownership to an admin group, delegate management without full ownership, and audit who can access an object.
codeExamples.breakdown: OWNER TO assigns full control to a group. MANAGE lets stewards administer grants on the schema without owning it. The service principal receives only the privileges its job needs (least privilege). INFORMATION_SCHEMA and SHOW GRANTS provide auditable views of effective access.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Ownership of orders moves to sales-admins; sales-stewards can manage grants on prod.sales; etl-prod-sp can write to orders only; the audit queries list current grants.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Leaving ownership with a departed individual locks future grant changes; over-granting the service principal (e.g., catalog-wide MODIFY); confusing MANAGE (administer grants) with ownership (full control including DROP).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Standardize ownership on admin groups, use MANAGE for delegated stewardship, and codify all of this in Terraform so it is reviewable and reproducible.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A company must give analysts read access to curated sales data, give engineers write access to the same schema, give an ETL job scoped write access, and prove to auditors that no individual has standing access outside their role.
endToEndExample.inputData: A Unity Catalog catalog 'prod' with schema 'prod.sales' containing tables orders, customers, and line_items; IdP groups data-analysts, data-engineers, sales-admins, and a service principal etl-prod-sp.
endToEndExample.architecture: Account-level Unity Catalog metastore shared across workspaces, groups synced via SCIM from the corporate IdP, grants codified in Terraform, and audit via system tables and INFORMATION_SCHEMA.
processingSteps: 1. Sync organizational roles to Unity Catalog groups via SCIM (no per-user grants).
2. Grant USE CATALOG on prod and USE SCHEMA on prod.sales to data-analysts and data-engineers.
3. Grant SELECT on schema prod.sales to data-analysts (inherited by all tables) for read-only access.
4. Grant SELECT, MODIFY, and CREATE TABLE on prod.sales to data-engineers.
5. Set ownership of the schema and tables to sales-admins; grant scoped MODIFY on target tables to etl-prod-sp.
6. Run SHOW GRANTS and query INFORMATION_SCHEMA to confirm the effective access matches the design.
endToEndExample.output: A least-privilege access model where analysts read, engineers read/write/create, the ETL service principal writes only its targets, and an admin group owns the objects.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Audit logs and system tables record every grant/revoke and access; periodic access reviews compare actual grants against the role design.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If a user lacks a traversal privilege, queries fail with a clear permission error; misconfigurations are corrected by adjusting group grants (not user grants), and Terraform drift detection flags out-of-band changes.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Access is consistent across workspaces, scales by group membership, and is fully auditable, satisfying compliance reviewers that least privilege is enforced and that no individual holds standing out-of-role access.

industryUseCases.problem: Clinical analysts need de-identified data while billing teams need financial data, and access must be provably restricted for HIPAA audits.
industryUseCases.solution: Separate catalogs/schemas per data domain with group-based grants (clinical-analysts, billing-team) and ownership held by a governance group; least privilege enforced via USE + SELECT.
industryUseCases.benefits: Provable compliance, simple onboarding/offboarding via group membership, and clear audit trails of who can access protected health information.

industryUseCases.company: Financial institution (SOX and segregation of duties)
industryUseCases.problem: Regulators require that the team producing financial data cannot also approve it, and that access is segregated by role.
industryUseCases.solution: Distinct groups for producers (MODIFY on staging) and consumers (SELECT on curated), with ownership in a controls group and service principals for automated reconciliation jobs.
industryUseCases.benefits: Enforced segregation of duties, reduced insider risk, and audit-ready evidence of role-based access for SOX controls.

industryUseCases.problem: Dozens of teams across many workspaces previously managed inconsistent per-cluster ACLs, causing access drift and security gaps.
industryUseCases.solution: Centralized Unity Catalog metastore with IdP-synced groups, catalog/schema-level grants with inheritance, and Terraform-managed RBAC.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent, reproducible access across all workspaces, dramatically reduced administrative toil, and a single source of truth for governance.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Group-based grants plus hierarchical inheritance let one statement cover thousands of users and all current/future objects in a catalog or schema, so governance scales with headcount and table count without grant explosion.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Because Unity Catalog operates at the account level, the access model is independent of any single workspace and persists through workspace recreation or failure.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Unity Catalog is a managed, highly available control plane; authorization is a fast metadata check that does not add meaningful latency to queries.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Codifying all grants and ownership in Terraform/SQL makes the entire RBAC configuration reproducible, so it can be re-applied to a recovered or new metastore quickly.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Authorization checks are lightweight metadata operations; keeping group structures clean and using schema-level inheritance minimizes the number of grants the system must evaluate.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Group-based RBAC minimizes the number of grant objects and the manual effort of access administration and audits, lowering operational cost and reducing breach-related risk.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Enforce default-deny and least privilege, grant only to groups, reserve ownership/MANAGE for small admin groups, and layer row filters and column masks on top of RBAC for fine-grained protection.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use SHOW GRANTS, INFORMATION_SCHEMA privilege views, and Unity Catalog audit logs/system tables to continuously verify effective access and detect drift.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Periodic access reviews and Terraform drift detection ensure granted access still matches the intended role design and that no out-of-band grants have crept in.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Centralize Unity Catalog audit logs and alert on sensitive grant changes (e.g., new SELECT on a PII catalog, ownership transfers, or grants to individual users).

recommendedPractices: **Grant to groups, not users:** Map roles to IdP-synced groups and control access purely via group membership.
**Apply least privilege and default-deny:** Grant only the minimal privileges each role needs; everything else is denied.
**Use inheritance deliberately:** Grant at catalog/schema level for whole-domain roles; reserve object-level grants for exceptions.
**Own with admin groups:** Assign object ownership to small admin groups, never to individuals, so access management survives personnel changes.
engineeringStandards: Every data-access role corresponds to a group; no standing privileges are granted to individual users.
Traversal privileges (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA) are granted alongside any object privilege, or the object grant is considered incomplete.
All grants and ownership are codified in Terraform/SQL and reviewed via pull requests, with drift detection enabled.
designRecommendations: Model catalogs/schemas around data domains and environments (e.g., prod, dev) to make domain-level grants meaningful.
Separate read, write, and admin roles into distinct groups to support segregation of duties.
Use service principals with narrowly scoped privileges for automated jobs.
namingConventions: Name groups by role and domain, e.g., sales-analysts-ro, sales-engineers-rw, sales-admins.
Name service principals by purpose and environment, e.g., etl-sales-prod-sp.
documentationStandards: Maintain a role-to-privilege matrix mapping each group to its grants and objects.
Document ownership for each catalog/schema and the rationale for any object-level exceptions.
Record the IdP-to-group mapping and the SCIM sync configuration.
testingStrategies: After provisioning, run SHOW GRANTS and INFORMATION_SCHEMA queries to assert effective access matches the design.
Use test users in each group to verify both allowed and denied operations behave as expected.
Run Terraform plan in CI to detect unintended grant or ownership changes before they reach production.

commonMistakes.mistake: Granting SELECT on a table without USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parents.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers assume a table grant is self-contained, as in some legacy systems.
commonMistakes.impact: The principal cannot see or query the object and gets a confusing permission error despite holding SELECT.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always grant the traversal privileges (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA) on every ancestor together with the object privilege.

commonMistakes.mistake: Granting privileges directly to individual users.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It feels quicker for a one-off request than configuring a group.
commonMistakes.impact: Per-user grants proliferate, become inconsistent, complicate audits, and are easy to forget at offboarding, leaving standing access.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Grant only to groups synced from the IdP and manage individual access exclusively by group membership.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assigning object ownership to an individual.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The person who created the object becomes its default owner and it is never reassigned.
commonMistakes.impact: When that person leaves or changes teams, no one can manage or re-grant the object, creating an access deadlock.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Transfer ownership to a small admin/steward group with ALTER TABLE ... OWNER TO `group`, and use MANAGE for delegated administration.

comparisonSection.explanation: RBAC grants access based on a principal's role/group membership and the object identity; it is simple, auditable, and scales via inheritance, but cannot natively express context. ABAC decides access using attributes of the user, resource, and environment (e.g., region, clearance, time), enabling fine-grained, context-aware rules at the cost of more complex policy management. Databricks is primarily RBAC, but you achieve ABAC-like behavior by combining RBAC with row filters and column masks that use functions like is_account_group_member().

Group grants attach privileges to a role; membership (synced from the IdP) determines who has access, so onboarding/offboarding is just membership changes and audits are simple. User grants attach privileges to a specific person, which is quick for one-offs but proliferates, drifts out of sync, and leaves standing access at offboarding. Best practice is group grants for essentially all production access.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a principal, a securable object, and a privilege in Unity Catalog?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A principal is the identity receiving access (user, group, or service principal). A securable object is the thing being protected (catalog, schema, table, view, function, volume, etc.) referenced in the three-level namespace catalog.schema.object. A privilege is the allowed action (SELECT, MODIFY, USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, CREATE, EXECUTE).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: These three are the who, what, and what-action of every GRANT statement. Mention the three-level namespace as a distinguishing Unity Catalog feature.

beginnerQuestions.question: Why should you grant privileges to groups rather than individual users?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Group-based grants make access scalable and consistent: you manage access by changing group membership, audits are simple, and offboarding removes access automatically when a person leaves the group. Per-user grants proliferate, drift, and are easy to forget.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This is the single most-tested RBAC best practice. Tie it to IdP/SCIM sync and least privilege.

intermediateQuestions.question: A user has SELECT on a table but still cannot query it. Why?
intermediateQuestions.answer: They are missing the traversal privileges on the ancestors: USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the schema. In Unity Catalog you must be able to traverse to an object before any object-level privilege takes effect.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This is the classic gotcha. Emphasize that USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA do not grant data access themselves; they are necessary traversal privileges.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does privilege inheritance work, and how does it interact with REVOKE?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Privileges granted on a catalog or schema are inherited by current and future child objects, so one grant can cover an entire domain. REVOKE removes a specific grant but does not override a broader grant: if a user still has SELECT at the schema level, revoking it on a single table will not block access because the schema-level grant is inherited.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show understanding that effective access is the union of all applicable grants, so you must revoke at the level where the grant was made.

advancedQuestions.question: Design a least-privilege RBAC scheme for prod and dev catalogs serving analysts, engineers, an ETL job, and a governance team.
advancedQuestions.answer: Create IdP groups: analysts (USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA + SELECT on curated schemas), engineers (adds MODIFY and CREATE in dev and staging schemas), governance (ownership/MANAGE on catalogs), and a service principal etl-prod-sp with USE + scoped MODIFY only on its target tables. Grant at schema level via inheritance, assign ownership to the governance group, restrict prod writes to the service principal and a small set, and codify everything in Terraform with audit via INFORMATION_SCHEMA.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Look for least privilege, group-based grants, ownership by a group, traversal privileges, inheritance, separation of duties between prod and dev, and auditability.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you implement attribute/context-aware access (e.g., region-restricted rows) when Databricks RBAC is role-based?
advancedQuestions.answer: Combine RBAC with Unity Catalog row filters and column masks that call is_account_group_member(). RBAC grants the role access to the table; a row-filter function then restricts visible rows based on the querying user's group membership (e.g., only rows where region matches the user's regional group), and column masks redact PII for non-privileged groups. This layers ABAC-like behavior on top of the RBAC foundation.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrates the boundary of pure RBAC and the correct Databricks pattern of composing RBAC with row/column policies for fine-grained control.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: An engineer who owned several production tables has left the company, and now no one can alter or grant access on those tables.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The root cause is individual ownership creating a single point of failure. A metastore admin or current owner must transfer ownership to a group, then enforce a policy that ownership is always group-based going forward.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: As a metastore admin, run ALTER TABLE prod.sales.<t> OWNER TO `sales-admins` for each affected object to restore manageability, then audit for other individually owned objects and reassign them to admin groups, and codify ownership in Terraform so future objects are created/owned by groups.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the Unity Catalog RBAC architecture for a multinational company with regional teams, strict compliance, and dozens of Databricks workspaces.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use a single account-level metastore shared across workspaces. Organize catalogs by environment and domain (prod_sales, dev_sales). Sync regional and functional roles as groups from the IdP via SCIM. Grant USE + SELECT/MODIFY at schema level by group, assign ownership to regional governance groups, and add row filters/column masks using is_account_group_member for region- and PII-scoped access. Codify all grants in Terraform.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Schema-level inheritance simplifies management but requires careful schema design; combining RBAC with row/column policies adds power but increases policy complexity; central metastore standardizes governance but requires disciplined group hygiene.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Add teams and tables without new grants by relying on group membership and inheritance; review access periodically via INFORMATION_SCHEMA and audit logs; use Terraform drift detection to keep the live state aligned with the declared policy across all workspaces.

followUpQuestions: What is the difference between MANAGE and ownership on a securable object?
Which privileges are required to create a new table in a schema?
How do service principals differ from users in an RBAC design?
How do you audit all privileges a given group holds across a catalog?
Why does Databricks recommend account-level identity federation for groups?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Unity Catalog RBAC grants privileges (SELECT, MODIFY, USE CATALOG/SCHEMA, CREATE, EXECUTE) to principals (users, groups, service principals) on securable objects in a catalog.schema.object hierarchy, with top-down inheritance and object ownership, best applied via groups under least privilege.
keyConcepts: Principals: users, groups, service principals (grant to groups).
Traversal: USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA required before any object privilege works.
Inheritance: catalog/schema grants apply to current and future children.
Ownership: full control; assign to admin groups, never individuals.
commands: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod TO `data-analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA prod.sales TO `data-analysts`;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders TO `data-analysts`;
GRANT SELECT, MODIFY ON SCHEMA prod.sales TO `data-engineers`;  -- inherited by tables
REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders FROM `data-analysts`;
interviewPoints: USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA are mandatory traversal privileges, not data access.
Always grant to groups, never individuals; manage access by membership.
Privileges inherit downward; effective access is the union of all grants.
Ownership confers full control and must live on admin groups.
Combine RBAC with row filters/column masks for ABAC-like fine-grained control.
quickNotes: Effective privilege = union of direct grants and all group grants (recursive).
REVOKE removes a specific grant; broader inherited grants still apply.
MANAGE delegates grant administration without transferring ownership.
Service principals carry scoped privileges for non-interactive jobs.
Codify grants in Terraform and audit via INFORMATION_SCHEMA and audit logs.

keyTakeaways: Unity Catalog RBAC is built from three pieces: principals (who), securable objects in the catalog.schema.object namespace (what), and privileges (which action), connected by GRANT/REVOKE.
Access requires both the object privilege and the traversal privileges USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its ancestors; SELECT alone is never enough.
Privileges inherit top-down (catalog -> schema -> object) so a single schema-level grant can cover all current and future tables, and effective access is the union of all applicable grants.
The cardinal best practice is group-based, least-privilege RBAC: grant to IdP-synced groups, assign ownership to admin groups, and never give standing privileges or ownership to individuals.
Pure RBAC is role-based, not context-aware; for attribute-driven rules like region-scoped rows or PII masking, layer row filters and column masks using is_account_group_member on top of RBAC.
